title: The Liking Gap in Conversations: Do People Like Us More Than We Think?
rawText:
We recruited two people to have a conversation.
people systematically underestimated how much their conversation partners liked them and enjoyed their company

claims.text: Compare reciprocal liking after a conversation
claims.quote: We recruited two people to have a conversation.
people systematically underestimated how much their conversation partners liked them and enjoyed their company

proposals: Consider optional mutual follow-up after a real conversation. Ask a group organizer whether uncertainty prevents newcomers from reconnecting. The study did not test this adaptation or return attendance.

title: Why a Simple Act of Kindness Is Not as Simple as It Seems
rawText:
Five studies explored this possibility.
compliment givers underestimated how positively the person receiving their compliment would feel

claims.text: Five studies of predicted compliment reception

claims.quote: compliment givers underestimated how positively the person receiving their compliment would feel

proposals: Consider an optional prompt to appreciate someone's observed contribution. First ask newcomers whether this would feel welcome. Evidence here is abstract-only; durable friendship and return attendance were not established.

title: Some Thing to Talk About? Differential Story Utility From Experiential and Material Purchases
rawText:
In eight studies
people believe they derive more happiness from talking about experiential purchases

claims.text: Eight studies of experiential and material purchases
Reported value of talking about experiential purchases
claims.quote: people believe they derive more happiness from talking about experiential purchases

proposals: Consider a memorable-moment conversation prompt after a shared activity. Ask the organizer if this gives newcomers something useful to discuss. This is an extrapolation from purchase-related ratings, not a demonstrated friendship or retention intervention.
